title: Collections.checkedList/Map/Set — runtime type enforcement, catching heap pollution

s1_definition.profdef: `Collections.checkedList(list, String.class)` wraps a list with runtime type checking — every `add()` and `set()` call verifies the element IS the declared type, throwing `ClassCastException` at INSERT time (not later at GET time). This catches heap pollution from raw types or unchecked casts IMMEDIATELY when the wrong type is inserted. Without checked wrapper: wrong type sneaks in via raw code → CCE happens later at GET time → hard to debug. With checked wrapper: CCE at ADD time → stack trace points directly to the buggy code.
s1_definition.analogy: Normal list = open filing drawer. Someone puts a sandwich (Integer) in the cheque drawer (List<String>) through a back door (raw type) → you discover it MONTHS later when you grab it. Checked list = filing drawer with a TYPE SCANNER at the door. Every item scanned on entry: "Is this a String? No → REJECT immediately with alarm!" The bug is caught AT THE DOOR, not months later.
s1_definition.oneliner: checkedList/Map/Set = runtime type check on every insert. ClassCastException at ADD time (not GET time). Use to catch heap pollution from legacy raw-type code.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto Collections.checkedList runtime type enforcement. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how Collections.checkedList runtime type enforcement solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a checked collection of account IDs created with `Collections.checkedList(list, String.class)` to enforce type safety at runtime.

**Step 1.** Rajesh's valid String account ID "SAV2001" is added, and the checked wrapper verifies the type matches String before storing it.

**Step 2.** A raw-typed reference tries to insert a non-String (heap pollution), and the checked wrapper immediately throws `ClassCastException` at the point of insertion.

**Step 3.** Because the bad value never enters the collection, later reads of Priya's and Rajesh's IDs stay clean, so the type violation is caught early instead of corrupting downstream logic.
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: Rajesh SAV2001 (Rs.1,000,000), Priya CUR3001 (Rs.250,000)
    │
    ▼
  Service layer (applies Collections.checkedList runtime type enforcement)
    │  loads accounts into the collection
    │  performs the operation (add / lookup / order / dedup)
    ▼
  Collection state changes
    │  SAV2001 and CUR3001 processed with BigDecimal amounts
    ▼
  Output: correct result returned to the caller
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`Collections.checkedList/Map/Set` wraps a collection with runtime type checking on every insert operation. Without it: heap pollution from raw types causes ClassCastException at GET time — the stack trace points to the get() call, not the buggy add(). With checked wrapper: ClassCastException at ADD time — the stack trace points directly to the code that inserted the wrong type. Use when integrating with legacy raw-type code, debugging mysterious ClassCastExceptions, or as a safety net during migration from raw types to generics. Performance cost: one `instanceof` check per add — negligible for most use cases. In banking: wrapping collections passed to legacy modules — `Collections.checkedList(accounts, Account.class)` catches any type violation immediately.

---

keyPoints: Wraps a list with runtime type checking on every add/set
Catches heap pollution at the point of insertion — not later at retrieval
Collections.checkedList(list, String.class): only String elements allowed
Useful for debugging — finding where wrong types are inserted
